tagline: Your cluster state lives in Git, and every rollout is a diff you can read.
overview: The cluster should look exactly like the repository says it does, and nothing should change it by accident. We set up a reconciler — ArgoCD or Flux — that watches your manifests and pulls them into the cluster, so a manual kubectl edit is corrected automatically instead of quietly becoming production. Configuration arrives through review, not through someone's terminal history.

Releases then move in steps rather than all at once: a canary takes a slice of traffic, a blue/green switch holds both versions live for a few minutes, and a feature flag separates deploy from release entirely. Rollback is a revert of the commit that caused the drift, applied by the same reconciler that rolled it out.
problems: Someone edits a live cluster and nobody knows it happened
Staging has drifted so far from production that tests mean nothing
A bad release takes an hour of emergency kubectl to undo
Environment promotion depends on one engineer's memory and a wiki page

includes.title: Declarative desired state
includes.text: Application and environment configuration described as manifests, so what should be running is readable, diffable and reviewable before it ever reaches a cluster.

includes.title: Continuous reconciliation
includes.text: ArgoCD or Flux compares live resources against the repository on a loop and corrects drift within minutes, including changes made by hand during an incident.

includes.title: Progressive rollouts
includes.text: Canary and blue/green strategies release to a small share of traffic first, with automated promotion or abort driven by error rate and latency measurements.

includes.title: Feature flag control
includes.text: Flags let you deploy code dark and release it later per team, tenant or region, so a rollback can be a toggle rather than a deployment.

includes.title: Secrets out of Git
includes.text: Encrypted secrets with SOPS or External Secrets keep credentials out of plain manifests while still letting the reconciler inject them at deploy time.

includes.title: Rollout visibility
includes.text: Sync status, health and rollout history for every application in one view, so you can see which environments are behind before it becomes an outage.

deliverables: ArgoCD or Flux installed across every target cluster
Application manifests and environment overlays in a repository you own
Progressive rollout policy for canary and blue/green releases
Drift alerts wired into your existing on-call rotation
Runbook for rollback, sync failure and reconciler recovery

process.title: Audit current deploy paths
process.text: We list every way code and configuration currently reach a cluster, including scripts, consoles and manual steps, and mark which ones cause drift.

process.title: Model environments as overlays
process.text: Base manifests plus per-environment overlays for staging, production and any short-lived environments, so differences are explicit and reviewable.

process.title: Wire the reconciler
process.text: Install and harden ArgoCD or Flux, connect it to your repository, and configure sync policies, health checks and notification targets for failed reconciliations.

process.title: Rehearse rollout and rollback
process.text: We run a real progressive release and a real rollback in front of your team, then hand over the runbook and the alert routing.

faqs.a: It is most mature there, and that is where ArgoCD and Flux do their best work. You can apply the same pattern to Terraform with Atlantis or to virtual machines with a config manager, but the reconciliation loop is slower and less convincing outside a cluster.

faqs.q: What stops a developer from committing straight to production?
faqs.a: Branch protection plus a sync policy that only reconciles the main branch, with production promoting through an approved pull request. ArgoCD can also require a manual sync for sensitive environments, though most teams find that friction outweighs the safety once the review process is trusted.

faqs.q: How does this differ from the CI/CD work you do?
faqs.a: CI/CD covers the build, test and artifact stage that produces a version. GitOps picks up from there, deciding what that version should look like in each environment and keeping the cluster aligned with that decision. Most teams need both, and they share a repository.

faqs.q: Can we keep our existing Helm charts?
faqs.a: Yes, and we usually start there. Charts are rendered or used directly by the reconciler; we may add Kustomize overlays around them for environment-specific values. The migration is a change of delivery mechanism, not a rewrite of everything you have written.

seo.title: GitOps & Release Management — ArgoCD, Flux & Rollouts
seo.description: Git becomes the single source of truth for what runs where, with ArgoCD or Flux reconciliation, canary rollouts and a rollback that is one commit revert.
